To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have found a new technique for the analysis of the proteins of ribosomes and that this technique allows us to resolve the majority of the proteins of rabbit reticuocyte ribosomes.

(1) the number of proteins in the rabbit reticulocytic ribosome is 63, (2) the proteins are arranged in two-dimensional patterns, (3) these patterns can be used to identify the proteins of other ribosomes.

we have found 63 proteins in the rabbit ribosome, that we have determined the molecular weights of all these proteins, and that we have found that the proteins migrate into several bands in one-dimensional electophoresis, and that the number of bands increases to as many as 5 in two-dimensional electrophoreses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure of the ribosome.
the development and application of a new technique of two-dimensional electrophoreses to the analysis of proteins.
the study of the molecular biology of the ribosome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rabbit reticulocytes contain a total of 63 ribosomal proteins which are distributed among 4 or 4 1/2 subunits.
63 different polypeptide components of molecular weights from 12 000 to 50 000 have been resolved by this method.
there are 63 proteins in the 40 S subunit, 34 in the 60 S subunit and 2 in the ribosomal core.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
63 ribosomal proteins can be resolved in two-dimensional electrophoreses.
63 ribosomal proteins are present in the reticulocyte.
63 ribosomal proteins are present in the rabbit reticulocytes ribosome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can identify the proteins that are different between these two groups.
the number of proteins in a cell is not necessarily the number of proteins encoded by its genome.

the number of resolved ribosomal proteins is very close to the number of proteins that have been reported to be present in the ribosome, suggesting that we have resolved all of the ribosomal proteins.
